1. Discovering a Body of Work
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00837
The name of Haydar Amoli will already be familiar to readers of this book. We have referred to his writings more than once when discussing essential aspects of Twelver Shiism.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00838

In particular (Book I, Chapter III, §2), we drew attention to his interpretation of the Quranic verse (33:72) concerning the divine trust entrusted to humanity. That interpretation carries a further idea: the trust can be passed on only to someone who shows himself to be its rightful heir by being capable of receiving it. This is one of the Quranic verses on which the inner, esoteric understanding of Islam—and therefore Shiite Islam—is founded.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00839

Haydar Amoli's work brings us to the heart of a question that has arisen repeatedly in these pages, and that anyone seeking to recover Islamic esotericism at its source—the inner life of spiritual Islam—must confront.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00840

How does the spiritual knowledge (ʿirfān) of Sufism, now relatively familiar in the West, relate to Shiite spiritual knowledge or theosophy (ʿirfān-e shīʿī), which remains far less well known? The conviction of the Iranian ʿārif, the person who possesses this spiritual knowledge, is that Sufi gnosis could never have existed without Shiite gnosis before it. Its original source, they believe, lies in the teachings of the holy Imams, who explained to their disciples the hidden meaning of the Quranic verses.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00841

Taken as a whole, Haydar Amoli's writings are an outstanding expression of that position. They offer one of the clearest opportunities to study a form of Shiism fully conscious that, in its essence, it is Islam's inner or esoteric teaching. The great treatise we have recently published bears the title Jāmiʿ al-asrār, a Compendium of Esoteric Teachings.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00842

Haydar Amoli was neither an isolated figure nor the first in a succession of such thinkers. We have already observed that the secrecy to which Twelver Shiism was forced for several centuries means that we must allow for a great many people who were Shiites in secret; it also helps explain why relatively few works of this kind have survived.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00843

Even so, in the thirteenth century Sa'doddin Hamuyeh and his disciples were already prominent representatives of Shiite Sufism, or Sufi Shiism. In the following century—the eighth century of the Islamic calendar, the fourteenth of the Christian era—Haydar Amoli, although he belonged to no particular ṭarīqa or Sufi order, deserved, alongside a few others such as Rajeb Borsi, the description given to him in the title of this chapter.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00844

The pages devoted to him here are intended only as a brief introduction to his writings, pending the translations and studies they deserve. His work is one of the keys to the hidden spiritual dwelling of Twelver Shiism.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00845
We shall begin by outlining its meaning and its place among the full body of Shiite writings.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00846

We shall then recount how we were led to discover the work of Sayyed Haydar Amoli, and how a series of fortunate manuscript discoveries enabled us to reconstruct both his life and the list of his writings.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00847

As Haydar Amoli tells us in the opening pages of his great compendium of Shiite theosophy, the Jāmiʿ al-asrār, his central concern is to recall the original relationship between Sufism and Shiism, and consequently to set out a doctrine of Shiism that is not of his own invention but goes back to its very beginnings: to what the Imams taught their disciples and closest companions.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00848

Traditions (hadith) from the Imams are quoted abundantly throughout his work. Their teaching is the foundation of his thought and the authority to which he constantly returns. If he embraces Sufism, he does so out of fidelity to the Imams themselves. In this he differs both from Shiites concerned only with the outward meaning of religion and from Sufis who are not Shiites.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00849

Haydar Amoli's understanding of Shiism as the inner teaching of Islam has not merely endured from century to century. It is thoroughly alive today, and is shared by all the ʿurafāʾ, those devoted to spiritual knowledge. I have heard it expressed repeatedly, not only by venerable shaykhs but also by young mullahs.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00850

One had only to ask, for example, why Shiism has no missionary spirit, why it does not try to win converts. The answer invariably expressed the same conviction: if the Imam does not guide a person inwardly, then whatever words you address to that person, however sublime, will reach their ear as no more than a passing breath of wind.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00851

As for someone guided by the inward Imam, let that Imam guide them. For this reason I was repeatedly reminded that Shiism, in its essence, is an inward initiation: an initiation into the inner meaning of Islam's highest teachings, handed down and enriched through a long tradition from one century to the next. Although Shiism addresses everyone, a young mullah told me, its meaning and vocation are to bring forth, little by little and across the centuries, a spiritual elite.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00852

Did the Imams not say again and again, “Our cause is difficult and heavy to bear; only an angel brought near to God, a prophet sent on a mission, or a believer whose heart has been tested can bear it”? To become a religion of the masses, then, would put Shiism in danger of being reduced to the ẓāhir, its outward aspect, until it was nothing more than a particular rite alongside the other legal traditions of Islam. One may of course object that since the Safavid period such a transformation into a mass religion has already taken place.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00853

But that is precisely the question to which these inexhaustible conversations continually return. In exchanges of this kind, I have heard young mullahs display a profound awareness of their spiritual task, however difficult its immediate future may be. They may be few, and even less widely recognized.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00854

But was their situation not already foreseen in the First Imam's conversations with Komayl ibn Ziyad? At the very least, these young men bore witness that the silsilat al-ʿirfān, the lineage of spiritual knowledge, would not be broken.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00855

Haydar Amoli's work shows, perhaps better than any other, that a tradition remains alive only through continual spiritual rebirth. The spirit of tradition remains truly a spirit only while it is creative; without that creative spirit, tradition would be little more than a funeral procession. Here, “creative” describes the activity that follows from unceasing inspiration (ilhām). Without such inspiration, the living interpretation of the sacred Book could not disclose what had remained hidden. This idea belongs with the notion of continuous creation (tajdīd al-khalq). Spiritual interpretation is a source of perpetual renewal.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00856

But renewal is not the same as innovation: innovation implies, in one way or another, a break with what came before, or an act of force. What makes these renewals “original” is precisely that each returns to the origins. For a long time, Western studies of Sufism were conducted in such a way that Haydar Amoli's views on Shiism and Sufism might strike a Western scholar, at first, as an unprecedented innovation.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00857

Yet his purpose is essentially to restore the tradition of Islam in its fullness: an Islam embracing both the ẓāhir, the outward meaning, and the bāṭin, the inward meaning. For him, this fullness is the very meaning of Shiism. Unfortunately, we have already had reason to regret how badly Shiite thought and theology have long been treated in the West.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00858

A certain scholarly conformism accepted as an unquestioned premise that everything in Shiism was “tendentious,” when it did not go so far as to use frankly insulting descriptions, such as those that somehow found their way into the writings of Nöldeke. Others claimed to explain everything through “political intrigues” and “social facts,” even turning Shiism into a political creation of the Safavid age.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00859

Yet politics scarcely figures in the Imams' teachings. More than a century before the Safavids, Haydar Amoli's writings show Shiite thought capable of constructing its own great systematic works—so much so that the major writings of the Safavid era can no longer be studied without reference to our Sayyed.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00860

We must return to the essential point. The Imams' teaching requires us to attend to the religious meaning of Shiism: in its essence, it is a phenomenon of spiritual life. This religious meaning sustains both a spiritual experience and a metaphysics that give shape to vast inner worlds.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00861

We will not discover it through troublemakers or agitators. No one has ever succeeded in preventing such people from making careers for themselves, not even in the circle surrounding the Imams. We need only avoid confusing them with what is truly at issue. Once we learn to see what is at issue, the statements made by Haydar Amoli and thinkers like him about Sufism will no longer surprise us.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00862

But if we insist on reducing everything to secular terms, we close off a sanctuary of Islamic consciousness and radically distort any possible study of religious experience as it is lived and understood. Perhaps the consequences of that distortion have already spread to the East, among a generation educated in Western schools. If so, Haydar Amoli's work may appear more relevant than ever.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00863

The significance of his work becomes clear when we consider the purpose that guided him from early youth, as he himself confides to his readers. Drawing on the texts, he wanted to remind them that the holy Imams' teaching certainly explains many obscure details of the sharīʿa, the religious law, but that in its essence this teaching is directed toward the inward meaning (bāṭin), from which it cannot be separated.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00864

When the Imams' explanations are systematically gathered around each Quranic verse to form a continuous commentary, their teaching becomes a guide to the “seven hidden depths of Quranic Revelation.” Unfortunately, some people who called themselves Shiites failed to recognize this teaching. Some wanted to retain only what concerned law and ritual.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00865

Why, then, did so much of what the Imams taught about the inner dimension—the hidden, spiritual meaning, the asrār or mysteries, the bāṭin—bear fruit instead in non-Shiite Sufism? It was this paradox that led Haydar Amoli, at the very beginning of his great book, to formulate a corresponding paradox of his own: “The Sufis are those who truly deserve the name of Shiites (al-shīʿa al-ḥaqīqīya) and of believers whose hearts have been tested (muʾmin mumtaḥan).”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00866

A Shiite Sufi, of course, will have no difficulty accepting this claim. It has borne fruit throughout the centuries; much of Ma'sum Ali-Shah's great encyclopedia of Sufism amounts, in effect, to an extended commentary upon it.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00867

But a Shiite who rejects esoteric knowledge (ʿirfān) and confines religion to its outward meaning will find the claim much harder to accept. As Haydar Amoli himself puts it, it is a “hard blow.” There are doubtless also Shiite spiritual teachers of the kind we have already mentioned—mystics in the fullest and most genuine sense of the word—who would wish to qualify the statement. They maintain a certain reserve toward Sufism, preferring to speak of ʿirfān, spiritual knowledge, rather than taṣawwuf, Sufism.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00868

Even Molla Sadra Shirazi, whose work is steeped in the spirit of Sufism—or perhaps precisely because it is—wrote a vigorous attack on a certain kind of Sufism: the Kasr aṣnām al-jāhiliyya, or Shattering the Idols of Ignorance.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00869

Haydar Amoli himself shows the same clear judgment. He distinguishes one kind of Sufism from another, and does so without mincing his words. In him, clear sight and independence of mind go together. His attitude toward Ibn Arabi offers another example. He admires Ibn Arabi fervently, follows his teaching, and writes commentaries on his works.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00870

Indeed, he was among the Shiites who did most to bring Ibn Arabi's thought into the Shiite tradition. For these thinkers recognized something of their own intellectual and spiritual inheritance in Ibn Arabi's theosophy. Many of his chapters—those on Salman Pak or the Twelve Imams, for example—might have been written by a Shiite.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00871

Yet on one question Haydar Amoli firmly refuses to follow him. His criticism is respectful but persistent and uncompromising, because the issue bears directly on the Shiite understanding of prophecy and of the Imams. Who is the “Seal” (Khātim) of the walāya, the spiritual authority and guardianship transmitted through the Imams? Haydar Amoli devotes considerable attention to criticizing Ibn Arabi's position on this question—a position perhaps made more daring still by Ibn Arabi's commentator Dawud Qaysari.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00872

The criticism is important both in his great theosophical compendium, the Jāmiʿ al-asrār, and in the introduction to his extensive commentary on the Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam, the treatise read and reread, generation after generation, by spiritually minded Muslims.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00873

In short, the idea governing our Sayyed's thought is this. On the one hand, the Shiism of the Twelve Imams is Islam in its esoteric fullness: spiritual religion, the true meaning of Revelation, the spiritual knowledge at the heart of Islam. Insofar as Sufism also upholds this inward teaching, while certain Shiites reject it for one reason or another, we may say that Sufism is true Shiism—its representative, as it were, incognito within Sunni Islam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00874

On the other hand, Sufism has unfortunately sometimes lost sight of its origins and fallen into serious errors, particularly over the identity of the “Seal of the walāya.” The process is easy to understand. Sufism received the very idea of walāya from Shiism. To separate itself from Shiism and claim independence, it therefore had to alter that idea at its roots. Many Sufis are unaware of this. They denounce Shiism, forgetting that it is the source of their own ʿirfān.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00875

Some maintain that the inward meaning (bāṭin) can eventually dispense with the outward meaning (ẓāhir), and that mystical truth (ḥaqīqa) releases a person from the obligation to observe the religious law (sharīʿa). These are two related errors, whose excess mirrors an opposite excess: that of Shiites who think they can dispense with spiritual knowledge altogether. They imagine that the outward sense, by itself and without any inward sense, is the true meaning of religion. Such people, in the end, are Shiites only figuratively (majāzī), not in the fullest sense of the word.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00876

Haydar Amoli thus conducts his struggle on two fronts. He challenges those who recognize nothing beyond a literal reading of religion as law, whether they are Sunni or Shiite. And he challenges Sufis who have forgotten the origins and implications of their own spiritual knowledge, and of the consecration symbolized by the Sufi cloak (khirqa) that they wear. This was his life's work. It also helps us place him within the four periods we have proposed, here and elsewhere, for understanding the dramatic history of Shiism.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00877

Any adequate division into periods ought, above all, to take account of Shiite thought and spirituality as they unfold into a world of their own, with a history of its own. That history is a hierohistory—a sacred history whose meaning is shaped by the divine. Because it is always oriented toward the ultimate fulfilment of things, it must break through history in the ordinary sense whenever the two meet.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00878

Any scheme based simply on the outward succession of dates and events can therefore describe only the external aspects of this spiritual world; it remains outside sacred history itself. For the reader's convenience, I shall briefly recall the broad outline of the four periods we distinguish in the outward history of Twelver Shiite thought.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00879
First: the initial period, that of the holy Imams and their immediate disciples, ending with the “Greater Occultation” (Ghaybat al-Kubrā) of the Twelfth Imam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00880
Second: the period from Kolayni (d. 329/940), who compiled the great collection of traditions from the Imams, to the philosopher, theologian, and astronomer Nasir al-Din Tusi (d. 672/1274).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00881

Third: the Mongol period, extending from Nasir Tusi to Mir Damad and the School of Isfahan in the eleventh Islamic/seventeenth Christian century. Fourth: the period from Mir Damad to our own day, when another period may perhaps be beginning.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00882

Sayyed Haydar Amoli, living in the eighth Islamic/fourteenth Christian century, is thus a leading figure of the third period. Now that some of his major works are known to us, we can say that they tower over the philosophical, theological, and theosophical writing of his century.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00883

What, then, is the decisive feature of Shiite thought during this third period, both in its content and in the form it takes? It seems we may answer, briefly, that the defining development was precisely the one mentioned a few lines ago: the integration of Ibn Arabi's thought into Shiite thought.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00884

Ibn Arabi died in 1240. We have already indicated the exact question on which Haydar Amoli, despite his extraordinary reverence for Ibn Arabi, puts forward a decisive criticism: the identity of the person who is the “Seal of the walāya”—in other words, the identity of the Imam. We have had occasion to mention this criticism before.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00885

Nonetheless, in Haydar Amoli's work, as in that of Ibn Abi Jomhur in the following century, the entire metaphysics of being, the understanding of tawḥīd (divine unity) in its two aspects, outward and inward, the doctrine of the divine Names and the forms in which they become manifest (maẓāhir), and hence the whole elaboration of the teaching concerning the Imams—all these extend and deepen Ibn Arabi's doctrines.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00886

The fact remains, too, that Ibn Arabi's immense body of work has educated spiritually minded Muslims generation after generation. His short compendium, the Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam (The Bezels of the Wisdoms of the Prophets), has been the subject of some 150 commentaries. Around 130 of their authors, writing in Arabic or Persian, were Iranian. Some commentators were Sunnis, others Shiites. Haydar Amoli's extensive and highly individual commentary stands among the foremost works of the latter group.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00887

We said earlier that Haydar Amoli's work, together with that of Ibn Abi Jomhur, did more than almost any other to integrate Ibn Arabi's thought into Shiite thought, as though Shiism were recovering something that already belonged to it from Ibn Arabi's immense intellectual legacy.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00888

This raises the whole question of the origins and sources of the thought of the Shaykh al-Akbar, the “Greatest Master.” Future research will have to pursue the question through both Ibn Arabi's own writings and the surviving works of Shiite philosophy. It concerns Ibn Arabi's early influences and education during his youth in Andalusia, and the spread of both Ismaili and Twelver Shiism among the spiritual teachers of Andalusia—above all Ibn Masarra and the School of Almeria, whose teachings Asín Palacios was able to reconstruct from quotations in Ibn Arabi himself.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00889

One begins to discern an extraordinary cycle: Shiite thought travelling as far as the westernmost lands of Islam, then returning to the East through Ibn Arabi, who could no longer live and think as a theosopher under the conditions prevailing in Andalusia. Ibn Arabi might even have reached Iran himself had the upheaval of the Mongol invasions not kept him away.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00890

But just a century after his death in Damascus, a young Iranian Sayyed left his native land—the city of Amol and the shores of the Caspian Sea—and settled at the holy places of Shiism in Iraq. There he would become perhaps the most outstanding Shiite commentator on Ibn Arabi, the thinker who, above all others, would lead the theosophy of the Shaykh al-Akbar back to what he believed to be its source.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00891

This brings us to the stages of our own discovery of Sayyed Haydar Amoli's writings. We have described them elsewhere, on the occasion of the first publication of two of his major treatises, and shall recall only the essentials here.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00892

Our path was guided by two interests that came together: Ibn Arabi's work and Shiite thought. Frequent quotations in the authors we were studying suggested to us that Haydar Amoli's writings ought to be among the first approached by anyone wishing to understand that Shiite thought which permeates the philosophy and spirituality of Iranian Islam, where philosophical reflection retained a vitality and momentum unknown elsewhere in the Islamic world.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00893

After locating two of his treatises in Iran and obtaining photocopies, we therefore devoted several years of research and teaching to his work. Eventually we found ourselves in the anxious predicament familiar to so many scholars: vita brevis—life is short. We were convinced that we must publish those of our Sayyed's writings which were accessible to us and which we had already translated to a considerable extent.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00894

Yet other equally urgent tasks made us hesitate to undertake so monumental a project alone. It was then that Osman Yahia, a leading specialist in Ibn Arabi who shared our assessment of Haydar Amoli's importance, kindly offered to collaborate.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00895
His help put an end to our hesitation, and work on the edition began.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00896

Moreover, Osman Yahia's own research led to discoveries of inestimable value. In Istanbul, he found Haydar Amoli's great commentary on Ibn Arabi's Fuṣūṣ. In Najaf, Iraq, among the treasures preserved at the Imam's shrine, he discovered the autograph manuscript of Haydar Amoli's great tafsīr: his extensive Shiite mystical commentary on the Quran, in seven substantial volumes. It is a monumental work of taʾwīl, the spiritual interpretation of scripture whose importance to philosophical thought in Shiite Islam we have stressed throughout this book.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00897

Six volumes of the author's own manuscript are at Najaf; the first is at Qom, where a copy of the opening of the commentary is also kept in the library of Sayyed Shihaboddin Mar'ashi Najafi, who generously placed it at our disposal. At Najaf, the collection is completed by the autograph of the last treatise composed by Sayyed Haydar, the Treatise on the Higher Sciences (Risālat al-ʿulūm al-ʿāliya), whose importance is not hard to imagine.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00898

Furthermore, the introductory writings to his commentary on Ibn Arabi and the opening of his Quranic commentary contain two autobiographical accounts that complement one another. Together they reveal the spiritual drama our Sayyed lived through and the radical decision by which he resolved it. They also provide detailed titles of his writings and allow us to arrange them chronologically over the course of his life. There are thirty-four works, written in Arabic and Persian. Some are short treatises; others are vast works filling several volumes.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00899
We would be completely satisfied as researchers if we had already found manuscripts of every one of our author's works. Unfortunately, we have not yet reached that point.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00900

But there is another possibility, all too rare, in which an author's own account of his life brings his writings closer to us. We then long to find the surroundings in which he lived, meditated, and worked, and sometimes that wish can be fulfilled.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00901

In Isfahan, for instance, we can revisit the Sadr madrasa, the college where Mir Damad taught and where Sadra Shirazi and so many others spent their student years. In Shiraz we can revisit the Khan madrasa, where that same Molla Sadra taught, including the room in which he gave his lessons and the place he occupied there. With Sayyed Haydar Amoli, things are more difficult, at least as far as the Iranian period of his life is concerned.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00902

We shall see that before the great rupture dividing his life into two periods, he spent most of his youth in Amol, in his native Tabarestan. The upheavals of history, and the storms unleashed by the Mongols, have left few ancient monuments standing there.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00903

Nevertheless, those of us preparing the edition of Haydar Amoli's works were eager to make a pilgrimage together to Amol and the shores of the Caspian Sea. A new road, opened only a few years earlier, cuts directly through the Alborz mountains and brings one from Tehran to Amol, immediately to the north, in a journey of some two hundred kilometres.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00904

We went in search of buildings that Sayyed Haydar might have known or visited in his lifetime. Only one seems likely: the imamzadeh, a shrine known in local tradition by several names, including Seh Sayyed (“the Three Sayyeds”) and Mir Haydar. The mausoleum stands in a garden beside a stream and is generally dated to the seventh Islamic/thirteenth Christian century or the eighth Islamic/fourteenth Christian century. Our Sayyed probably knew it. The same cannot be said of any other surviving monument.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00905

Today the banks of the Haraz River (Harāz Rūd), which runs through Amol, have been pleasantly landscaped. What did they look like when Amol was the capital of the princes of Tabarestan? One thing certainly remains: the landscape. There is the forest clothing the mountain slopes, from which the road emerges onto the broad plain of Mazandaran; the exuberant greenery, so different from the austerity of Iran's high plateau; the shifting moods of the sky, changing with those of the sea, held captive here within the continent.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00906

Sayyed Haydar could have seen all this much as we see it, allowing for a few differences. Perhaps we need to see it with him if we are to hear the full resonance of the moving confession translated below: that of a young man who possessed everything and who, at thirty, chose to abandon it all and become nothing more than a “pilgrim toward God.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00907

His decision coincided with a dramatic moment in the history of Mazandaran, which includes Tabarestan—a name formerly applied especially to its mountainous region. Biographical reference works often call our Sayyed “Amoli Mazandarani.” Through his family's standing and the duties he performed in his youth at the court of his ruler, his life became linked to one of Mazandaran's most celebrated dynasties, the Bawandids, descendants of Bawand.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00908

When he recalls the prince he served, he proudly emphasizes the dynasty's noble descent from the Sasanians of pre-Islamic Persia. Throughout the centuries, names of purely Iranian origin, borrowed from the heroes of the national epic, stood alongside Islamic names among the rulers of this house.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00909

A few essential facts will help place the autobiographical account we shall examine below. The Bawandids ruled Tabarestan for seven centuries, from 45/665 to 750/1349. Their descent was traced back to the Sasanians, through Parwiz, Andeshrawan, and Yazdgard. The dynasty comprised three successive branches.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00910

The third, the Kinkhwariyan, ruled from 635/1237–38 to 750/1349 and began with Hosamoddawleh Ardashir ibn Kinkhwar. His eighth successor and the dynasty's last sovereign was Fakhroddawleh Hasan ibn Shah Kay-Khosraw ibn Yazdgard, who ruled for sixteen years, from 734 to 750 of the Islamic calendar. It was this prince who welcomed Sayyed Haydar into his intimate circle and then appointed him minister.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00911

We shall see our Sayyed recall both the prince and his father with deep feeling. Fakhroddawleh had succeeded his own brother, Sharaf al-Moluk ibn Shah Kay-Khosraw, whose short but fortunate reign lasted six years and who died in 734/1333–34. At that time Sayyed Haydar was a boy of fourteen or fifteen; it is therefore unsurprising that his memory of this prince was equally vivid.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00912

Fakhroddawleh had married the sister of Kiya Afrasiyab of Cholab. Afrasiyab brought a false accusation against him before the religious scholars (ʿulamāʾ), using it as a pretext for the prince's murder. Fakhroddawleh was treacherously assassinated by his brother-in-law, or by the latter's two sons, on 27 Muharram 750/17 April 1349. It is almost as if the name Afrasiyab had destined its bearer, ever since the heroic age, to the sinister role of traitor.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00913

Fakhroddawleh left four sons and a daughter. The eldest, Malek Ka'us, was only ten when his father died. Those loyal to the dynasty failed to recapture Amol, but Afrasiyab would enjoy the fruits of his crime for only about ten years.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00914

These details belong to the path by which we are coming to know Sayyed Haydar Amoli and his writings. In the very year, 750/1349, when his prince was murdered and the Bawandid dynasty came to an end, Haydar decided to abandon his brilliant worldly career and “turn toward God.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00915

Yet although he describes in detail the spiritual circumstances that brought his conversion to its decisive conclusion, he says not a word about the tragedy that ended the dynasty in that same year. If we weigh the wording of his autobiographical account, it seems likely that he made his decision a little before the tragedy took place, while he was still a minister at the court of Amol.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00916

Much later, when he wrote two accounts of his life, he could speak of his ruler in the past tense, offering only a fervent blessing and saying nothing of his violent end. All this was already far behind him. Did he ever see his native Mazandaran again, where Tamerlane's Mongol horsemen were preparing to sweep through? We know nothing of his death. He takes his leave of us quietly with his final book, the Treatise on the Higher Sciences (787/1385–86).

2. An Autobiographical and Bibliographical Outline
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00917
We have just mentioned two autobiographical accounts through which the course of Sayyed Haydar Amoli's life comes clearly into view.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00918
We shall call them Autobiography A and Autobiography B.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00919

The earlier of the two, Autobiography A, appears at the beginning of the great Tafsīr ʿirfānī, the mystical commentary on the Quran entitled al-Muḥīṭ al-aʿẓam (The Supreme Ocean), which Haydar Amoli completed in 777/1375–76. It gives enough detail for us to glimpse his years of learning and his youth, as well as the reasons for the momentous decision that sent him out as a solitary pilgrim along the roads of Iran toward the Shiite holy places in Iraq.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00920

Unfortunately, the narrative breaks off abruptly at the bottom of its last surviving leaf, just as the author is describing in detail his extended stay in Isfahan on the way to Mecca. Was the writing interrupted and never resumed? Were pages torn out? Or were they simply misplaced when the manuscript was bound? Only a prolonged examination of the photocopies will allow us to decide. Whatever the explanation, this break currently deprives us of the fuller information that our Sayyed undoubtedly intended to give us there about the second period of his life.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00921

The second account, Autobiography B, is found in the introductory sections of the Naṣṣ al-nuṣūṣ, Haydar Amoli's commentary on Ibn Arabi's Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam, which he completed at Najaf in 782/1380–81. Here he reviews his youth and the spiritual crisis that led him to set out as a pilgrim toward the Holy Places, but in briefer terms than in Autobiography A. This time, however, the account does not break off.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00922

Instead, the author goes on to survey his activity as a writer, providing a catalogue of his works that is of inestimable value to us. By bringing the two narratives together, we can obtain an overall outline of his life. We have distinguished an Iranian period ending with his conversion (750/1349–50) and an Iraqi period beginning with his arrival at the Holy Places (751/1350–51). The Iraqi period, in turn, can be divided in two on the basis of the dates supplied by his writings.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00923
We shall therefore consider three periods in Sayyed Haydar Amoli's life, which we shall designate A, B, and C.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00924

Autobiography B allows us to establish the year of Sayyed Haydar's birth at Amol to within a year: 720/1320 (possibly 719 of the Islamic calendar, but more probably 720). We learn from it that he reached the holy places of Iraq in 751/1350–51. Allowing a year between his departure from Amol and his arrival there, he must have left the Caspian shores in 750/1349–50. He tells us that he was then thirty years old. Those first thirty years constitute the Iranian period of his life.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00925

Sayyed Haydar ibn Ali ibn Haydar Obaydi Hosayni Amoli belonged to a distinguished family of Sayyeds in Amol, a city whose population had been almost entirely Shiite from the earliest times. During this Iranian period he received his education and gained his first experience of life.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00926

In his great theosophical compendium, the Jāmiʿ al-asrār, he confides that from his youth—even from childhood—he had devoted himself passionately to the study of Twelver Shiite spiritual knowledge and theosophy (ʿirfān-e shīʿī-e davāzdah Imām). For this whole period, Autobiography A gives us the clearest portrait of his character, tracing the distinctive features of his spiritual and moral personality. Here we shall simply summarize it.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00927

The reverence Haydar Âmolî felt for his status as a Sayyed—a descendant of the holy Imams—led him to begin by tracing his family line. Generation by generation, it reached back to the Fourth Imam, Zayn al-’Âbidîn, son of the Third Imam, Hosayn, the martyr of Karbala.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00928

As he also tells us in his Jâmi’ al-asrâr, from childhood until the age of thirty he devoted himself to studying “the teachings of my forefathers, the immaculate Imams,” though at first he confined himself to the outward, religious-law aspect of the sharî’at. He then completed the full course of traditional learning, both transmitted and rational (manqûl and ma’qûl): theology based on received authority and speculative philosophy. He began his studies in Âmol, then travelled to Khorasan and studied at Astarâbâd; from there he went to Isfahan, where he remained for a considerable time. All these studies, begun in early childhood and pursued in Âmol and elsewhere, had occupied some twenty years.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00929

Sayyed Haydar therefore returned to his native Âmol when he was about twenty-five. Tabarestan was then ruled by Fakhroddawleh Hasan, son of Shâh Kay-Khosraw ibn Yazdgard, whose place in the Bâwandiyân dynasty we have already discussed. Sayyed Haydar himself explicitly recalls the origins of this dynasty. The pride with which this Shiite Sayyed emphasizes that his princes could trace their ancestry, generation after generation, back to the Sasanian rulers of pre-Islamic Persia is especially revealing of Iranian Shiite consciousness: a feeling of loyalty to both lines of descent, that of the Imams and that of the princes of ancient Persia.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00930

King Fakhroddawleh showered Sayyed Haydar with favors. He admitted him to his intimate circle, made him his confidant, and eventually appointed him minister. Our Sayyed seems then to have enjoyed every pleasure the world could offer: family life, honors, wealth, power, social connections, fine houses, agreeable companions and friends. His many allusions suggest that nothing was denied him.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-00931

Yet, as so often happens in accounts of spiritual conversion, it was in the very midst of this life of abundance, with everything promising what we would now call “a brilliant career,” that Haydar Âmolî discovered its emptiness, its taste of ashes. “So it continued,” he writes, “until, in the innermost secrecy of my being, the calls of Truth finally prevailed, and God revealed to me the vanity of the heedlessness, ignorance, and unawareness in which I was living.
